title: Dilbert Misreads End Construction Sign
situation: Dilbert drives alone and muses aloud about how no one could possibly object to building more roads. He then notes that whenever he sees highway construction, a protester has already put up a sign. The final panel shows a sign reading 'End Construction' at the side of a dirt road.
punchline: Dilbert mistakes a standard road-works 'End Construction' sign for a protester's message, showing how obliviously he assumes he understands the world.
summary: A driver naively wonders why anyone would resist new highways, then takes an ordinary roadwork sign for a protest placard.

title: Marriage Odds Versus Terrorist Odds
situation: Dilbert sits in an armchair reading a magazine and shares a survey statistic about the odds of a woman over 35 marrying versus being killed by a terrorist. Dogbert asks how many of those who do marry end up marrying terrorists. Dilbert answers one in four, and Dogbert says 'Gosh.'
punchline: Taking the survey's claim that marriage and terrorist death are equally likely, the dialogue deadpans that a quarter of the women who marry end up marrying terrorists, mocking the absurdity of the statistic and misuse of survey math.
summary: Two friends turn a grim survey about older women's marriage prospects into an absurd chain of reasoning about who they might end up wedding.

title: Dogbert Invents Exotic Birds
situation: Dilbert and Dogbert are birdwatching with binoculars. Dogbert excitedly reports spotting many exotic birds while Dilbert has only seen a robin. When Dilbert asks how that is possible, Dogbert shouts about a ridiculous made-up bird and Dilbert whips around to look for it.
punchline: Dogbert is clearly making up his bird sightings, and Dilbert proves how gullible he is by eagerly looking for an absurdly named bird.
summary: A birdwatching outing reveals that one participant is inventing wildly exotic species while the other falls for the silliest one.

title: Dogbert Glues Suction Cups on Kitten
situation: Dilbert confronts Dogbert, who is relaxing on a pillow next to a radio playing music. He says the neighbor reported that Dogbert glued suction cups onto their new kitten and stuck it on a car windshield. Dogbert responds by guessing the problem is copyright infringement, and Dilbert sarcastically asks for a second guess.
punchline: Dogbert, having done something obviously cruel, can only think the objection is a legal technicality like copyright infringement, ignoring the plain animal cruelty, which Dilbert points out by asking for a second guess.
summary: Dilbert scolds his dog for turning a neighbor's kitten into a windshield ornament, and the dog cluelessly wonders if it's an intellectual property issue.

title: Dilbert Fights Hunger With Bumper Sticker
situation: Dilbert announces to Dogbert that he is done talking about world hunger and is ready to take real action, dismissing those who merely debate policy. Dogbert, lounging on a green chair, guesses that his idea of action is buying a smug bumper sticker, and Dilbert proudly confirms it.
punchline: Dilbert's grand call to action turns out to be a trivial gesture of buying a bumper sticker, which mocks token activism that substitutes for real effort.
summary: After announcing a bold move to end talking and start acting on global hunger, Dilbert reveals his plan is to buy a self-righteous bumper sticker.

title: Dogbert Becomes a Substitute Teacher
situation: Dogbert tells a surprised Dilbert that he has landed a job as a substitute school teacher. Dilbert objects that Dogbert is a dog and unqualified, and Dogbert replies that small children won't notice. Dilbert then admits Dogbert reminds him of his fourth grade teacher, and Dogbert slyly asks if that's just coincidence.
punchline: Dilbert's fourth grade teacher may have been a dog too, implying that unqualified canine teachers have already been fooling children for years.
summary: A canine con artist takes a classroom job and hints that he may have been teaching kids for a long time already.

title: Dilbert and Eve: Nothing to Wear
situation: In the first panel Dilbert sits in an armchair, lecturing Dogbert that women have always played hard to get. The second panel, captioned 'Dilbert and Eve', shows Dilbert in the Garden of Eden with a snake draped around his neck, asking a naked Eve for a date next year. She declines by saying she has nothing to wear.
punchline: Eve's excuse that she has nothing to wear is a classic brush-off line, but it is literally true because she is in the Garden of Eden, so the rejection is both a joke about dating and about Adam and Eve's nakedness.
summary: A man's theory about hard-to-get women plays out in paradise, where the first woman turns him down with a wardrobe excuse that happens to be literally accurate.

title: Dogbert Sings the Greens
situation: Dilbert hears noise and finds Dogbert sitting on a small rug strumming a guitar. Dogbert explains he is singing the "greens," a cheerful cousin of the blues with the same beat. He then performs a song whose lyrics complain about trivial everyday annoyances.
punchline: Blues songs lament serious hardship, while Dogbert's "greens" are sung about petty first-world inconveniences like a car needing a tune-up and oversleeping by ten minutes.
summary: A guitar-strumming dog performs a mock-blues number about minor, trivial troubles to show how much less gloomy it is than the real thing.

title: Dogbert Loses Employee of the Month
situation: Dogbert, playing the role of Dilbert's employee, demands a new wage and benefits package and argues he works around the clock. Dilbert's answer is to hold a recognition scheme, and Dogbert is named Employee of the Month, as displayed on the refrigerator. Dilbert then reveals the award barely beat a kitchen appliance.
punchline: The 'Employee of the Month' honor is worthless because Dogbert only narrowly beat a toaster, mocking hollow recognition programs used in place of real pay raises.
summary: A pet demanding better pay is fobbed off with a token award that he won by a hair over a kitchen appliance.

title: Naked in a Garbage Can
situation: Dilbert wakes up naked and sitting in a garbage can and asks Dogbert why. Dogbert offers two explanations: Dilbert was killed by wild deer and cloned back to life from his old garbage, or he is using the can as a cheap above-ground pool. Dilbert hopes the second one is the answer.
punchline: Dogbert's second explanation is the mundane, cheapskate one, and it sounds almost as absurd as the cloning story, so Dilbert is left hoping for the lesser embarrassment.
summary: A confused, unclothed Dilbert gets two equally ridiculous explanations from his dog for waking up in a trash bin.

title: Dilbert Drives Toward Roadkill Blob
situation: Dilbert drives down a road while narrating his growing curiosity about something lying ahead, which he first guesses is a squished animal. He admits he doesn't want to look but can't resist, then is horrified, only to discover it's just an old shoe. Moments later he spots another small blob in the road and Dogbert, riding beside him, says it's his brain.
punchline: Dogbert implies that Dilbert's brain has fallen out of his head, mocking his panicky, overwrought reaction to a harmless old shoe.
summary: A driver works himself into a panic over an object in the road that turns out to be a shoe, and his canine passenger then quips that the next speck on the pavement is the driver's missing brain.

title: Elbonia Upgraded to Second World
situation: Dilbert reads a newspaper story saying Elbonia has been reclassified from a third-world to a second-world country. Dogbert asks what 'second' means, and Dilbert explains it as having plenty of food but not liking it. In Elbonia, a tall-hatted man is served a tray of airline food and complains.
punchline: Being 'second-world' is treated like economy-class air travel, so Elbonia's upgrade means they get plenty of food, but it's only bland airline meals.
summary: A country's move up in the world rankings is reimagined as a downgrade to tedious in-flight meals.

title: Rat Disguised as Tiny Kangaroo
situation: Ratbert sits on a chair and confides in Dogbert, who listens silently like a therapist. Ratbert explains that he once tried to escape the stigma of being a rat by painting a pouch on his belly and pretending to be a tiny kangaroo. He concludes that people hate tiny kangaroos too.
punchline: Ratbert's disguise failed because the prejudice wasn't about being a rat in particular; people simply dislike small, unwelcome creatures, so changing his appearance did nothing.
summary: A rat recounts his failed attempt to dodge public disdain by faking a marsupial pouch, only to discover the disguise earned the same contempt.

title: Random Drug Testing Blood Loophole
situation: A manager announces the company will begin random drug testing while Dilbert and a coworker listen. He notes that searching employees' cars or homes would be illegal, but says the company sees no ethical problem with drawing their blood. He adds that the results will be posted publicly in the cafeteria.
punchline: Management's ethics are absurdly selective: searching your car is off-limits, but extracting your blood is fine, and the results will be publicly displayed with no regard for privacy.
summary: A manager cheerfully explains that the firm's new drug screening takes blood instead of searching property, then promises to publish everyone's results for all to see.

title: Executive Claims To Be Normal, Smarter
situation: Dilbert sits quietly at lunch while an off-panel executive tries to assure him that he is just a regular guy. He admits to a higher salary and a nice office, then tacks on that he is far smarter than Dilbert. Dilbert says nothing throughout.
punchline: The executive's attempt at humble relatability collapses into condescending arrogance, revealing he believes his rank reflects superior intelligence.
summary: A boss-level lunch host insists he is an ordinary person, then steadily lists every way he considers himself better than his guest.

title: Dogbert Watches Solar Flare News
situation: Dogbert sits in an armchair watching a television news broadcast. The anchor reports on solar flares, then CNN's Wolf Blitzer is shown on the scene, reporting that it is another hot day on the sun. Dogbert responds with a thought bubble.
punchline: Dogbert is annoyed by the sun's blazing heat and calls it a bunch of show-offs, as though it were flaunting its temperature at everyone else.
summary: A dog watching the evening news mutters a grumpy retort at the sun for flaring up and making a spectacle of itself.

title: Airport Built From Leaf and Bee
situation: At a 'Rivers and Trees' management course, the instructor gives the participants an absurd creativity exercise: build a commercial airport landing strip using only a leaf and a dead bee. Before attempting anything, one participant announces that the group has already voted to split into design and construction teams, assigning the actual building to another group. The instructor simply calls time.
punchline: The managers spend their entire time on organizational politics and delegating the work rather than attempting the task, which shows how bureaucratic management thinking replaces actual creativity.
summary: A group at a corporate retreat wastes an impossible creative challenge by voting on who gets to design and who has to do the labor.

title: Dogbert Advertises Dilbert as Undesirable
situation: Dogbert, sitting in an armchair reading a newspaper, explains that he is testing his theory that good advertising can sell anything. He chose the least desirable thing on Earth as his product. The final panel shows a billboard advertising dates with Dilbert, while a woman looks at it and ponders.
punchline: Dogbert considers Dilbert the least desirable thing on Earth, so he uses him as the product to prove his advertising theory.
summary: A scheming dog launches a billboard campaign for a hopelessly unappealing product to prove that marketing can sell anything, and the product is his own owner.

title: Dilbert's Metal Detector Dating Plan
situation: Dilbert excitedly tells Dogbert he has found a new way to meet women: carrying a metal detector in the park. Dogbert sarcastically guesses he will dig up buried women with metal head plates, but Dilbert explains he is counting on women's scientific curiosity to start conversations, and he plans to collect phone numbers. Dogbert privately weighs helping him against the benefit of him never having children.
punchline: Dilbert's absurdly optimistic dating scheme is so hopeless that Dogbert concludes it might be better for humanity if Dilbert never reproduces.
summary: A hopeful engineer believes a metal detector will make him irresistible to curious women, while his dog quietly decides his genes are better off not being passed on.

title: Dilbert Offers House for Helga
situation: Dilbert is a salesman visiting a prospective client. The client says Dilbert's competitor already visited and promised a massage from Helga in exchange for the business. Dilbert, misunderstanding the going rate for bribes, offers his entire house for Helga, and the client notes he is new at this.
punchline: Dilbert wildly overbids with his own house for something the competitor offered as a simple massage, revealing that he is an inexperienced and naive salesman.
summary: A buyer reveals a rival's perk-based bribe, and a clueless salesman responds by offering far more than anyone would ever ask.

title: Employees Rank Ninth, Behind Carbon Paper
situation: The Boss addresses his staff at a meeting table and admits that his long-repeated claim that employees are the company's most valuable asset was wrong. He announces that money is the top asset and employees rank only ninth. When Wally nervously wonders what ranked eighth, the Boss reveals it was carbon paper.
punchline: Management's feel-good slogan about valuing employees is exposed as empty, since staff rank just below obsolete office supplies like carbon paper.
summary: A manager cheerfully admits that his staff are actually ranked ninth in importance, just beneath an outdated office supply.

title: Ratbert Flaps His Way Airborne
situation: Ratbert asks Bob the dinosaur whether Dilbert is right that you can't fly by flapping your arms. Bob says it depends on how hard you flap, so Ratbert flaps his arms wildly and ends up hovering in the air. Dilbert, reading a newspaper in an armchair, doesn't look up and insults Ratbert for being gullible.
punchline: Ratbert actually manages to fly by flapping, proving Dilbert wrong, but Dilbert nonchalantly insults him anyway, implying it's still embarrassing to be someone who would try this.
summary: A gullible rat takes a dinosaur's advice literally, flaps his arms until he floats, and is met with a flat insult from the unimpressed man reading the paper.

title: Boss Sends Dilbert to Elbonia
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he is being sent to the company's plant in Elbonia to teach the workers about quality, claiming he was chosen because he knows their language. Dilbert points out that they speak English, so the stated reason falls apart.
punchline: With his excuse debunked, the Boss cheerfully admits the real reason for the assignment is that he hates Dilbert, treating a punitive overseas posting as a punishment.
summary: A manager's flimsy justification for shipping an employee off to a remote foreign plant collapses, leaving only open spite as the motive.

title: Dogbert's Analogy-Padded Consulting Report
situation: Dogbert, working as a consultant, delivers a thick report on the company to The Boss. He admits he had no real insights, so he padded the document with witty analogies. The Boss reads a sample line, which insults his own pointy-haired head, and Dogbert asks if it is vivid.
punchline: The consultant's expensive report contains no actual insight, just filler analogies, one of which mocks the boss himself, and the boss is too clueless to object.
summary: A consultant dog hands over a hefty report with nothing useful inside except colorful similes, including a rude one about the client's own head.

title: Never So Little Measured So Much
situation: Dilbert hands his boss a growing stack of reports: a time report in fifteen-minute increments, a monthly project status, a budget forecast, key accomplishments and a jeopardy list. The boss happily collects the papers. In the last panel the boss, clutching the pile, thinks about how much is being measured.
punchline: The boss's own thought admits that the reporting is excessive for the tiny amount of actual work being measured, parodeying Churchill's famous line, yet he enjoys the paperwork anyway.
summary: An employee buries his manager in status paperwork while the manager privately jokes that the volume of measurement far exceeds the work being done.

title: Employee Dog Collar With Extension Cord
situation: The Boss hands Dilbert an employee locator device that tracks his location and restroom usage, and Dilbert realizes it is a dog collar. The Boss gloats that cubicles prepared workers for this, and Dilbert talks himself into accepting it. Just as he does, the Boss reveals the collar is powered by a six-foot extension cord, tethering him like a pet.
punchline: Just as Dilbert finishes rationalizing the humiliating dog collar, the Boss reveals it comes with a six-foot leash-like power cord, proving there is always a worse indignity.
summary: A manager outfits an engineer with a tracking collar, and the engineer's self-soothing excuses collapse when a short power cord turns it into a leash.

title: Dilbert Forgets His Technical Vocabulary
situation: Dogbert sits in a chair reading an article and informs Dilbert that a technical degree becomes obsolete in five years. Dilbert, busy at his computer, irritably asks him to stop interrupting while he works on something, but can't think of the technical term. He ends up calling it a 'doohickey', suggesting the article may be right.
punchline: Dilbert's inability to name the thing he's working on, falling back on the vague word 'doohickey', implies his technical knowledge has already gone obsolete.
summary: A dog reading about expiring degrees gets proof when the engineer he's pestering blanks on a technical term.

title: Boss Edits Insult Into Wording
situation: The Boss stands over Dilbert's desk holding his project status report. He reads aloud a line blaming the delay on a clueless, pointy-haired individual, which is obviously about him. His only feedback is a minor wording change, suggesting 'facilitated by' instead of 'due to'.
punchline: The Boss recognizes the insult is about himself but misses the point entirely, offering only a stylistic edit and proving his cluelessness.
summary: A manager critiques the phrasing of a report that mocks his own incompetence, fixing the grammar but ignoring the accusation.

title: Dogbert's Publishing House Rejects Everyone
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert how his new book publishing business is going. Dogbert happily explains that his favorite part is rejecting dozens of authors daily and insulting them. Dilbert points out that a publisher must eventually publish something, and Dogbert dismisses this as mere conventional wisdom.
punchline: Dogbert has built a publishing business around the fun of rejecting and insulting authors, and brushes off the core purpose of publishing as just conventional wisdom.
summary: A gleeful dog turns the power to reject aspiring writers into his whole business model and shrugs off the idea that a publisher should print books.

title: Ratbert Surveyed as Pencil Eraser
situation: Dogbert holds a clipboard and conducts a market research survey on Ratbert, who is sitting on the couch. Dogbert explains that Ratbert has been grouped into a market segment with wild fungi and pencil erasers. The first survey question asks whether he would enjoy having his head rubbed vigorously on paper, and Ratbert answers enthusiastically.
punchline: Ratbert is so naive that he cheerfully agrees to a question that treats him like a pencil eraser, showing how absurd and demeaning market segmentation can be.
summary: Dogbert surveys Ratbert after sorting him into an absurd consumer category, and the little guy happily plays along with a ridiculous question.

title: Daily Reports for Late Project
situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that the project is six weeks behind because the team is understaffed. The Boss ponders his options in a thought bubble, ruling out adding people, moving the deadline, and ignoring the problem. Dilbert then explains to Wally and Alice that the Boss's solution is to demand daily status reports.
punchline: Faced with a problem caused by too little staff, the Boss picks the one action that adds work and fixes nothing, making the team's situation worse.
summary: A manager who rules out every real remedy for a late, understaffed project settles on burdening the team with paperwork.

title: Freak Section: Choosing to Work
situation: A bald coworker peers over the cubicle wall and jokingly asks Dilbert what he's 'in for', treating the office like a prison. Dilbert insists he isn't a prisoner and works there by choice. The coworker concludes he's been seated in the section with the weirdos.
punchline: Dilbert's sincere claim that he chooses to work and likes it marks him as a freak, since everyone else sees the job as a prison sentence.
summary: Dilbert's neighbor treats the office like a jail, and learns his cubicle mate actually enjoys being there.

title: Saint Dogbert Sells Computing Enlightenment
situation: The Boss explains that he has asked Saint Dogbert, wearing a mitre and holding a bone staff, to settle a dispute over which computers the company should allow. Dogbert announces he will go to the desert to seek enlightenment about computing. In Palm Springs he is seen sitting at a table while vendor representatives with bags of money and cash line up to offer endorsement contracts, and he haughtily rejects one.
punchline: Dogbert's holy quest for the true path of computing is really a pretext to be bribed by competing vendors, and he treats the offers like an auction.
summary: A self-appointed saint is hired to judge a hardware dispute and promptly turns his spiritual retreat into a bidding war for paid endorsements.

title: Procurement Bob Substitutes Cheap Labeler
situation: The Boss trains Bob, a green dinosaur, for a procurement job. He tells him to treat every employee as a lying thief and hand out cheap substitutes to claim savings. An employee then comes to Bob after requesting a multimedia laptop and is given a Dymo label maker instead, and Bob accuses him of using a fake name.
punchline: Procurement is run on paranoia and fake savings, so employees get absurdly cheap substitutes for what they ask for and are accused of dishonesty for complaining.
summary: A newly hired purchasing clerk follows his boss's cynical advice and swaps a requested computer for a label maker.

title: Thinking Outside the Box, Literally
situation: Dilbert wants to think outside the box to produce a creative design, so he takes the idea literally and pushes his chair out of his cubicle into the hallway. The Boss walks up and tells him he is a fire hazard and must do his thinking inside his cubicle.
punchline: Dilbert takes the 'think outside the box' cliché literally, and the Boss shuts it down with the opposite rule, showing that management slogans about creativity collapse against petty rules.
summary: A designer who tries to be creative by moving his chair into the corridor is promptly ordered back into his cubicle by his supervisor.

title: Consultant Bills for Primal Screams
situation: Dogbert, wearing a beehive-style hat, performs poems and dances for the staff as a wellness consultant and asks Alice if it has healed her soul. Alice screams over the cubicle wall that she wants money, not dancing dogs. The Boss hears the outburst, concludes the primal screams are healthy, and asks Dogbert to teach him, so Dogbert hands him an invoice.
punchline: Dogbert turns an employee's angry scream of frustration into a new billable service by selling the Boss lessons in primal screaming.
summary: A consultant's wellness program provokes an employee's furious outburst, which the clueless manager mistakes for a therapeutic success and pays to learn.

title: Award for Trying the Door Knob
situation: The Boss complains that nobody in the group has been nominated for a special achievement award while other departments are giving themselves awards. After the team admits nobody has done anything notable, the Boss decides to lower standards. Later that month Alice receives an award for merely trying a locked door knob, and she is furious about being nominated.
punchline: With standards lowered far enough, the award goes to Alice for the trivial act of trying a locked door, which is hardly an achievement, and she is angry at the embarrassing recognition.
summary: A manager desperate to match other departments' honors ends up handing out an award for the most trivial act imaginable.

title: Planning to Fail Upward
situation: Wally gives a project update at a meeting, cheerfully explaining that his project began as a bad idea from senior management and is on track to become a spectacular failure. He reveals his plan is for people to forget the failure and remember only his experience, leading to promotions and a new romance. The Boss then asks if he has read the company mission statement.
punchline: Wally deliberately engineers a failing project because he knows failure is quickly forgotten while 'experience' gets rewarded, and he dismisses the company mission statement as something not to be taken literally.
summary: A cynical employee proudly reports that his doomed project is exactly on schedule to fail, counting on the failure being forgotten while his supposed experience earns him a promotion.

title: Shrinking a Cubicle, Quarter-Inch Weekly
situation: Carol catches Dilbert in the marketing department pushing against a cubicle wall. He explains that he secretly moves one man's cubicle wall inward by a quarter-inch every week as an experiment. When she asks what it is meant to prove, he admits he has forgotten because it has been going on so long, while the cramped occupant sits scowling in the foreground.
punchline: Dilbert has been slowly shrinking a coworker's cubicle for so long that he can no longer remember the purpose of the experiment, yet he keeps doing it.
summary: A prank-like experiment of gradually squeezing a coworker's workspace continues long after its original purpose has been forgotten.

title: Dogbert Teaches Phony Small Talk
situation: Dogbert runs a class on interpersonal skills and tells his students the secret to good relationships is being a huge phony. He drills them on three fundamentals: loud, simple and smiley. A student then loudly and cheerfully comments on a low-pressure system, and Dogbert asks him to repeat it using the word "weather."
punchline: The student follows the loud, smiley small-talk advice so literally that he uses obscure jargon instead of the simple word "weather," and Dogbert has to correct him.
summary: A dog instructor coaches his class on faking friendliness, and a student's enthusiastic small talk still manages to miss the point of keeping it simple.

title: Dogbert Invents Web Browser as Prank
situation: In a flashback, Dogbert and the world's smartest garbageman realize that the web browser they created as a practical joke has grown out of control. They wonder what happened to the college kid they framed for it. The final panel shows that kid, now fabulously rich, being groomed by a stylist while an assistant carries in a bushel of money and photographers wait nearby.
punchline: The college kid they framed as a prank became a wildly wealthy celebrity thanks to the web browser, so being framed turned out to be the best thing that ever happened to him.
summary: Two pranksters who accidentally unleashed the internet learn that their scapegoat has become a pampered, money-drowned star.

title: Dogbert Delivers Bad News With Jokes
situation: Dogbert announces to Dilbert that he is starting a business as a professional bearer of bad news, promising to find humor in tragedy. A woman then appears at the doorway and asks a riddle about her husband and the Village People. Dogbert delivers the bad news as the punchline: the Village People are coming back.
punchline: The riddle's answer reveals that the woman's husband is not coming back, either because he has left her or died, while the Village People are, which is both a dark joke and a delivery of bad news.
summary: A dog starts a service that breaks terrible tidings with a gag, and his first customer gets a darkly funny answer about her missing spouse.

title: Boss Highlights Only Page Numbers
situation: The Boss hands Alice a magazine article, proudly saying he highlighted the most important parts to save her time. Alice looks it over and points out that the only thing he highlighted was the page numbers. The Boss responds that it takes forever if you don't notice that.
punchline: The Boss's claim to save time is absurd because his highlighting is useless, and he deflects with a nonsensical excuse that treats his own mistake as a pitfall for the reader.
summary: A manager proudly hands over a marked-up article, but the only thing he marked was the page numbers, and he blames the reader's attention for any wasted time.

title: Cocky Applicant Gets Brushed Off
situation: Dilbert is interviewing a college student at a campus recruiting session. The student boasts of twelve better job offers and demands to know why she should work for Dilbert's company. Dilbert calmly says he'll see what he can do, then hands her his own résumé and asks if she has enough copies, reversing the roles.
punchline: Dilbert turns the tables by treating the arrogant applicant as a hiring helper, implying his own job prospects are so shaky he wants her to circulate his résumé to those twelve companies.
summary: A confident graduate brags about her many job offers, and the interviewer responds by quietly asking her to help him find a new job.

title: Focus Group of Loser Choices
situation: Dogbert, running a market research firm, addresses a focus group seated around a table. He reveals that the participants were chosen because they consistently make bad decisions, so his clients will do the opposite of what they recommend. The participants proudly cite their own poor choices, such as skipping jury duty and postponing a liver transplant to attend.
punchline: The participants prove they were perfectly screened for bad judgment by gleefully admitting they put a pointless focus group ahead of a civic duty and a life-saving operation.
summary: A research firm deliberately recruits people with terrible judgment for its panel, and the attendees immediately confirm their credentials with absurd life choices.

title: Skeptic Debunks Rat's ESP Claims
situation: A man with a mustache welcomes Dilbert, who has been sent by the Skeptics Association to debunk his pet rat's claims of ESP. The man explains that the other skeptics rarely go out since serving as jurors on the O.J. Simpson trial. Dilbert hangs up his coat and says he must hurry because he is also scheduled to debunk the Hubble telescope.
punchline: The skeptics are so reflexively dismissive that their schedule includes debunking even the Hubble telescope, an obviously real and verified instrument, and the O.J. jury reference implies they are the kind of people who reject evidence.
summary: A professional doubter arrives to dismiss a rat's psychic powers, then reveals he plans to dismiss a famous space telescope too.

title: Pharmacy Queue Strategy Meltdown
situation: Dilbert arrives at a pharmacy and can't tell whether there is one line or two, so he stands in the middle to hedge his bets. He mentally wills another customer to line up behind him, then competes with him to reach the faster cashier, finally shoving past him. When he reaches the counter, the cashier tells him he is in the wrong line and that stress medications are handled at the other one.
punchline: Dilbert's frantic, ruthless fight over a checkout line leaves him so stressed that he has ended up at the wrong counter, needing the very stress medication he was racing toward.
summary: A man's cutthroat scheming to win the fastest pharmacy line backfires when he learns he was queuing for the wrong service all along.

title: Alice Rewrites Manual With Drama
situation: Alice's draft of the user manual is being reviewed by Wally, who hands it back and complains that the characters in the examples were uninteresting and left him emotionally empty. Alice responds by revising it, rewriting the example users as the tragic figures of a romance, with user B unable to love user A because he is a bald engineer.
punchline: Alice takes the absurd feedback literally and sarcastically turns dry user manual examples into a melodramatic love story, mocking Wally with the fact that he himself is a bald engineer.
summary: A colleague is given a pointlessly emotional critique of a technical document and answers by writing a soap opera into it.

title: Headless New Guy's Pun Name
situation: Alice reads the driver's license of the new hire, who is a headless empty shirt and tie standing beside them. A bald, bespectacled coworker holding a coffee mug guesses the man's middle name is Lester, then reveals he was building a pun.
punchline: The name Edward Lester Mann sounds like 'headless man', which fits the new guy who literally has no head.
summary: A coworker steers a conversation about a new hire's name toward a groan-worthy pun on his missing head.

title: Terrible Ideas With Noble Excuses
situation: The Boss reads an announcement at a meeting that cubicle walls will be removed to improve communication. Dilbert wonders aloud why bad ideas always come with such noble-sounding justifications. The Boss, apparently missing the point, reads the next announcement: employees will be leashed and branded to improve morale.
punchline: Dilbert's complaint is proven right when the Boss immediately announces an absurdly cruel policy and dresses it up with a noble reason, showing he missed the sarcasm entirely.
summary: A manager cheerfully announces a string of awful workplace policies, each justified with lofty goals, and cannot see why an employee finds that suspicious.

title: Hired Yesterday, Now a Credenza
situation: The Boss tells Allen, a new employee hired just yesterday, that the salary budget has to be cut and he probably shouldn't have hired him. He then notes that there is spare money in the furniture budget. In the last panel Allen is on all fours with a lamp on his back, serving as a piece of office furniture, and thinks he will someday be a credenza.
punchline: Because furniture money is available while salary money is not, the employee is effectively kept on as office furniture, and his dream is to be promoted to an actual credenza.
summary: A freshly hired worker is told there's no payroll money for him but plenty for furniture, so he ends up serving as a lamp table and aspires to rise to credenza status.

title: Shipping Trash by FedEx Expenses
situation: Asok, carrying a box of old binders, asks Wally how to get them to the landfill quickly. Wally casually advises shipping them by FedEx and billing the cost to the Marketing department, since nobody there checks expense reports. Asok, stunned, thinks to himself that this is yet another thing he can never tell anyone about his job.
punchline: Wally's routine abuse of the expense system, sending garbage by overnight courier on someone else's budget, is so absurd and wasteful that Asok realizes his workplace is too embarrassing to describe to outsiders.
summary: A coworker learns that the office's standard method for disposing of junk is to courier it away at another department's expense.

title: Dilbert Calls Dogbert's Bathrobe Bluff
situation: Dogbert sits on the kitchen table and bets Dilbert a million dollars that he won't go to work dressed as he is, in a bathrobe over breakfast. Dilbert accepts the challenge and announces he is leaving right now. Dogbert, unbothered, thinks ahead to the argument that will follow over what the bet actually meant.
punchline: Dogbert never intended to pay up; he is already planning to weasel out of the bet by quibbling over the wording of the terms.
summary: A wager over wearing a robe to the office is met with confidence from one side and a cynical plan to dispute the rules from the other.

title: Whistle-Blower Bores Clueless Jury
situation: Dilbert is testifying as a whistle-blower, and his lawyer asks him to explain his employer's alleged crimes to the jury. Dilbert launches into technical jargon about applets and cookie data while the jurors look blank, bored or one sticks out his tongue. Dilbert complains about the jury, and the lawyer replies that the testimony has only made them hungry.
punchline: The jury doesn't understand the technical testimony and only hears 'cookie', so the lawyer says Dilbert has merely made them hungry.
summary: A whistle-blower's tech-heavy courtroom testimony leaves jurors baffled, with the word 'cookie' being the only thing that registers with them.

title: Boss Zaps Computer Board With Static
situation: The Boss proudly offers to demonstrate a 'technical trick' to a woman holding a circuit board from a parts box. He shuffles his feet and zaps the board with a static spark, and a 'zzzt' sound appears. In the last panel the board lies ruined on the floor, propping open a door.
punchline: The Boss's static shock fried the circuit board, leaving it useful only as a doorstop, which proves his technical ignorance and carelessness.
summary: A clueless manager shows off a static spark trick and destroys an electronic component, which ends up wedging a door open.

title: Six Weeks Without a Network
situation: The Boss shows a new employee to his cubicle and explains that the I.T. department won't connect him to the network for six weeks, so he can't do any real work until then. The Boss then cheerfully announces he will check in every few minutes to monitor what the employee is doing.
punchline: The Boss plans to constantly monitor an employee who has been given no tools to work with, which highlights the absurdity of demanding visible productivity while providing no means to be productive.
summary: A manager welcomes a new hire to a cubicle that is useless for weeks, then promises to hover over him constantly anyway.

title: Three Bullet Points, Invented Words
situation: Dilbert stands before an audience holding notes and explains that he was told to boil his whole project down to three bullet points. He says he had to invent new words to do it, then presents a slide listing three nonsense terms and warns that nobody wants to be any of them.
punchline: Condensing a complex project into three bullet points is so reductive that it requires made-up jargon, and the made-up labels sound like insults describing the people involved.
summary: Forced to compress an entire project into a tidy three-item list, Dilbert resorts to gibberish terms that he insists are unflattering to anyone they describe.

title: Pretending Chicken Sandwich Needs CPR
situation: The Boss stands beside Dilbert's desk and explains that he promised a bird protection society the company would not hurt any birds. He then mentions that the caterer served chicken sandwiches for lunch. He admits he got around the awkwardness by pretending to resuscitate his sandwich while actually eating it.
punchline: The Boss's absurd workaround to avoid hypocrisy, faking CPR on a chicken sandwich while eating it, shows how management satisfies the letter of a promise while ignoring its spirit.
summary: Having vowed to a bird-lovers group that the company won't harm birds, the boss deals with a lunch of chicken sandwiches by feigning to revive his meal while devouring it.

title: No Casual Days: Uncomfortable Clothes Policy
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, announces to an employee that casual dress days are cancelled because uncomfortable clothing supposedly makes people work harder. In the final panel the employee sits at his desk wearing a suit of armor while Dilbert stands beside him in a bulky spacesuit.
punchline: Taking the 'uncomfortable clothes boost productivity' logic to absurd extremes, the employees wear armor and a spacesuit and are too encumbered to actually do any work.
summary: An HR policy demanding miserable attire backfires when staff show up in clunky costumes that leave them motivated yet physically unable to function.

title: Deleting Files Instead of Adding Storage
situation: Dilbert confronts an IT support guy at his desk because he asked for more e-mail storage and instead had all his files deleted. The IT guy argues that he gets complaints whether he ignores requests or deletes files. Dilbert points out those are not the only two options, and the IT guy shrugs it off.
punchline: The IT guy frames his choices as only ignoring users or destroying their data, and then claims he can't please everyone, using a false dilemma to excuse his poor service.
summary: A tech support worker justifies wiping an employee's files by pretending his only alternative was to disregard the request.

title: Topper Can't Go First
situation: The Boss introduces Dilbert to a new employee, Topper, and brags that Topper can outdo anything anyone says about themselves. Dilbert tests this by simply asking how he is. Topper, whose whole act depends on responding to someone else's boast, admits he can't go first.
punchline: Topper's supposedly amazing ability to top anyone is just a one-trick gimmick that collapses the moment he has to speak first, so his 'system' is really just a dependence on others.
summary: A coworker billed as unbeatable at one-upmanship is undone by a simple greeting because his routine only works as a reply.

title: Elbonian Service Gets Grunted At
situation: Two tall-hatted, bearded Elbonians stand in mud holding tin-can string phones. One answers as the Elbonian Fulfillment Service and offers to 'thwart' the caller, who replies only with grunts. The agent then tires of the repeated joke, while a pig in the mud laughs with a tin can of its own.
punchline: The agent is fed up with the caller's endless, unfunny gag of grunting like a pig, and a pig on the line is the only one still laughing.
summary: A weary Elbonian help-desk worker on a tin-can phone refuses to indulge a prankster whose only contribution is animal noises.

title: Roofer Leaves Roof Off Before Rain
situation: A roofing contractor tells Dilbert, who is reading the newspaper, that he has removed the roof and will return next week to finish. When Dilbert asks what happens if it rains, the contractor shrugs it off and says he'll work indoors. Dilbert protests that his house will be ruined, and the contractor disclaims responsibility.
punchline: The contractor carelessly leaves the house exposed to the elements and then dodges all accountability for the foreseeable damage by claiming he can't control the weather.
summary: A home repairman strips off a homeowner's roof, leaves for a week, and brushes aside the obvious risk of a storm.

title: Buying Rave Movie Reviews From Dogbert
situation: The Boss phones Dogbert, who runs a review-for-hire service, to purchase a glowing review for his new movie. Dogbert quotes prices based on the praise phrases, as if they were menu items. The Boss then cleverly asks about the price of "best comedy so far this year" since his film opens on New Year's Day.
punchline: Movie blurbs are bought and sold like commodities, and the Boss tries to game the system by claiming "best of the year" praise for a film released on the first day of the year.
summary: A man shops for movie-poster praise from a dog who sells quotable superlatives at tiered prices, and tries to snag a bargain award for a January 1st release.

title: Starving the Homeless for Publicity
situation: Carol, holding a clipboard, tells Dilbert she is signing up volunteers to serve food to the homeless on Christmas Day. Dilbert wonders how the company can be sure the homeless will be especially hungry that day. Carol matter-of-factly reveals that the company's PR firm deliberately withholds food from them for two days before the news crews show up.
punchline: The company's charity photo-op is staged so cynically that its PR firm starves the homeless beforehand to make the volunteers' generosity look more dramatic on camera.
summary: A corporate holiday charity drive turns out to rely on a public relations firm deliberately keeping the needy hungry so the cameras get a better show.

title: Promotion That Means More Work
situation: The Boss announces to Dilbert that he is being 'promoted', but it turns out to mean only more work with no change in pay or title. The Boss insists it must be good news because he used the word promotion and is smiling, then holds a strained grin while Dilbert watches uneasily.
punchline: The Boss tries to make a pay-free workload increase sound like good news by relabeling it a promotion and forcing a smile, which only frightens Dilbert.
summary: A manager rebrands extra duties as an advancement and keeps a rigid grin to convince his employee it's a reward.

title: Boss Greets Everyone With Wrong Names
situation: Dilbert tries to raise a supplier problem with the Boss, who insists on a walk-and-talk. While Dilbert speaks, the Boss cheerfully waves at passing coworkers and greets them with names. Dilbert points out that the names are wrong, and the Boss admits he makes up names because it's easier.
punchline: The Boss doesn't bother learning his employees' names and just invents greetings, showing he is both inattentive to Dilbert's problem and indifferent to the people who work for him.
summary: A manager who won't stop to listen breezily hails passing staff with invented names and defends the habit as simpler.

title: Barrels Become the Company Dress Code
situation: The Boss, standing in a barrel, announces a new dress code of barrels as a cost-cutting measure. He then adds that Fridays will be casual barrel day. In the final panel, employees seated at a table in barrels with their arms sticking out complain that the barrel rides up when they sit.
punchline: The expense-cutting dress code is absurd, and the 'casual barrel day' exception mimics casual Friday, while employees are left dealing with the impractical consequences of wearing barrels.
summary: A manager imposes barrel-wearing on staff to save money, complete with a relaxed Friday policy, and the employees discover the practical downside while seated.

title: Moon Landing Analogy Gets Shot Down
situation: The Boss stands over Dilbert's desk and demands a computer built entirely from recycled paper, justifying it by pointing to the moon landing. Dilbert dismisses the comparison as a flawed analogy, and the Boss responds by telling him to phone the people who did the other impressive things. Dilbert fires back that those people probably use better analogies.
punchline: The Boss misses the point of Dilbert's criticism and sarcastically suggests asking others how they do it, while Dilbert retorts that the real difference is that they reason with good analogies.
summary: A boss defends an absurd paper-computer demand by comparing it to space travel, and his engineer mocks the logic twice over.

title: Bucket Brigade Corporate Social Responsibility
situation: Carol suggests the company show more corporate social responsibility, and the Boss first offers to cut her salary to give to the poor. When she asks to protect neither herself nor his stock options, he proposes polluting less, then assigns her to scoop sludge out of the river with a bucket. In the last panel Dilbert and Wally remark on the coffee tasting better.
punchline: The Boss's idea of reducing pollution is to have Carol bucket sludge out of the river by hand with nowhere to put it, while the coffee in the last panel is implied to be made with that polluted river water.
summary: A manager turns a request for social responsibility into a pointless manual cleanup chore, while two coworkers unknowingly enjoy coffee that seems suspiciously improved.

title: Execution Misunderstood: Staff Meeting Punishment
situation: Someone off-panel tells the Boss he must focus on execution, and the Boss takes it literally as executing people. Catbert, the evil HR director, advises him to make it look like an accident. The Boss then announces that his staff meetings will now last two hours, and his visibly distressed employees react in horror.
punchline: The Boss's idea of a deadly 'accident' is making staff meetings two hours long, implying that endless meetings are a form of torture that kills morale (and perhaps people).
summary: Misreading a call for effective follow-through as a call for killing, the boss settles on a slower cruelty: marathon staff meetings.

title: Layoffs Boost Morale, Then Firing
situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, lectures an employee standing before his desk about how layoffs improve morale and show management is decisive. The employee, persuaded, says he feels more optimistic. Catbert then announces that, secondly, the employee is fired.
punchline: The employee's newfound optimism from the pep talk is immediately crushed when the 'morale-boosting' speech turns out to be a prelude to his own layoff.
summary: A cat in charge of personnel sells a worker on the upside of downsizing and then promptly cuts him loose.

title: Consultant Learned By Getting Fired
situation: The Boss proudly introduces Nildo Orbfutz, an expensive consultant hired to calculate how much company time is wasted. Dilbert asks about his credentials and learns Nildo's only qualification is on-the-job training. Dilbert guesses Nildo was fired from every job for wasting time, and Nildo cheerfully confirms that this is how consulting works.
punchline: The consultant hired to measure wasted time is himself an expert in wasting time, having been fired from every job for it, and calls that the wonderful world of consulting.
summary: A pricey new consultant hired to uncover time-wasting turns out to have qualified for the role by being a chronic time-waster himself.

title: Therapist Diagnoses Dilbert's Spacetime Fold
situation: Dilbert lies on a couch telling his therapist he spent the week feeling like he was drifting through alternative universes. She asks whether he has been near dense objects that could fold space-time. A flashback shows the Boss standing over Dilbert at his desk, asking if there will be any unforeseen problems, while Dilbert panics.
punchline: The 'dense object' warping Dilbert's reality is the Boss, whose cluelessness and absurd questions leave Dilbert feeling like he has slipped into another universe.
summary: A therapist's physics-flavored diagnosis of a patient's disorientation is answered by a flashback revealing the real source: his dim-witted boss.

title: Boss Learns of Evil Merger
situation: During a meeting, a bald coworker reads a newspaper and angrily reports that the company is merging with an evil firm that intends to downsize them. Dilbert, Alice, and the others glare furious at the news. The Boss, seated across the table, calmly asks whether the paper printed his quote praising how valuable they are.
punchline: The Boss is only concerned about whether his flattering quote got printed, ignoring that the employees are about to be laid off, which implies his praise is hollow PR.
summary: Staff fume over a newspaper report of a layoff-minded merger while their manager only wonders if his compliment about them made the article.

title: Dogbert's Manipulation Advice Backfires Healthily
situation: Dogbert sits on the couch beside Dilbert and coaches him on manipulating people by lying about what others said, including a ready-made excuse if the victim checks with the source. Dilbert, holding a drink, objects that the advice sounds unhealthy. Dogbert answers by falsely claiming the Mayo Clinic said otherwise.
punchline: Dogbert immediately applies his own manipulation technique to Dilbert, lying about what a respected authority said to defend his unethical advice.
summary: A scheming dog tutors his owner in deceit and then uses that very trick to brush off the owner's doubts.

title: Collateral for Borrowing a Chair
situation: A man asks Dilbert if he can borrow his chair for a meeting. Dilbert agrees only if the man leaves his wallet, keys, company ID and a shoe as collateral. When the man points out he is the company's Chief Financial Officer, Dilbert responds by demanding even more items.
punchline: Dilbert treats a senior executive's request like a pawn-shop loan, and the man's high rank only makes Dilbert raise the collateral instead of relenting.
summary: Dilbert demands a pile of personal belongings as a deposit before lending his office chair, and refuses to ease up even when the borrower turns out to be a top executive.

title: Wally's Plausible Password Excuse
situation: Alice asks Wally for the approved vendor list and he claims it is online behind a password. Alice recognizes his habit of falsely saying information is on the net and predicts the excuses he will use next. Wally smugly sips his coffee and supplies the one she missed: the user name.
punchline: Alice lays out Wally's entire chain of stalling excuses, and Wally cheerfully adds one more, proving he is unashamedly working the system to avoid doing any work.
summary: A coworker anticipates every dodge a lazy colleague might use to avoid producing a document, and he happily hands her another one.

title: Tina's Email Personality Defense
situation: Dilbert confronts Tina about an abusive email she sent him. She apologizes and explains that her email personality is separate from her kind, gentle real-time personality. When Dilbert accepts this, she immediately turns back to her keyboard and snaps at him again, proving the hostile persona is still in charge.
punchline: Tina's claim of a separate gentle in-person personality is undercut when she instantly resumes her abusive tone the moment she's typing again.
summary: A coworker excuses her vicious emails as a separate persona, then promptly unleashes it again at her keyboard.

title: Meeting Won't End Despite Hints
situation: Dilbert sits in a meeting and taps his papers on the table, hoping his coworker will take the hint to end it. The coworker ignores the signal and keeps talking. In the last panel, Dilbert recounts the story to Dogbert, who is tipping an empty pitcher and says he already told a similar person it was all gone.
punchline: Subtle body-language hints don't work on oblivious people, so Dogbert's blunt statement that the coffee is all gone is the only thing that actually ends the conversation.
summary: A man shuffles his papers to politely end a meeting but his oblivious colleague keeps on talking, while Dogbert shows that bluntness is the only thing that works.

title: Change Is Good, Unless It's Pay
situation: The Boss lectures employees that change is good, using a slide with a smiley face. Dilbert volunteers to ask a question, suggesting the company triple everyone's pay as a change, then suggests the Boss work for free. The Boss gets angry, and afterward Wally gleefully recalls the Boss's outburst.
punchline: When Dilbert applies the Boss's 'change is good' slogan to pay and the Boss's own salary, the Boss cannot defend it and angrily blames Dilbert's logic for ruining his slogans.
summary: A manager's cheery pro-change slogan collapses when an employee applies it to salaries and the manager's own pay.

title: Karma Justifies Selling Defective Products
situation: Dilbert confesses he feels guilty because his company sells defective products. Dogbert offers a twisted take on karma, claiming he can harm people all day because he assumes they deserve it. Dilbert then asks where they are, and Dogbert says they've wandered into a bad doodle.
punchline: Dogbert's self-serving karma logic assumes everyone he wrongs deserves it, and the strip ends with the meta-joke that they are standing in a poorly drawn, bad doodle.
summary: Dogbert twists the idea of karma into a blanket excuse for mistreating people, then the pair realize they have strayed into a crudely drawn, surreal scene.

title: Goons Motivate Better Data Security
situation: Dilbert warns the Boss that Elbonian hackers are trying to steal the company's source code. The Boss suggests sending goons to beat them up, and when Dilbert proposes improving data security instead, the Boss threatens to have the goons beat up Dilbert unless he does. In the last panel, Dilbert works diligently at his computer while two goons loom over him and mock his firewall.
punchline: The Boss's threat of violence turns out to be an effective motivator, with Dilbert admitting it works and the goons absurdly critiquing his security work.
summary: Facing a hacking threat, a boss answers a request for better security with menace, and the thuggish supervision actually gets results.

title: One Sale Proves Massive Piracy
situation: Dilbert reports to The Boss that the company's total sales to Elbonia amount to a single software package, and concludes that Elbonians must be pirating software on a massive scale. The final panel shows an Elbonian standing in mud, holding a tiny Frisbee and telling his pig to leap and catch it in its mouth. The pig refuses and tells him to go first.
punchline: The Elbonians are so impoverished and primitive that their entertainment is a tiny Frisbee, so the idea that they are running a sophisticated software piracy operation is absurd.
summary: A sales report from a poor mud-dwelling country is interpreted as proof of rampant piracy, while the locals can barely afford a toy for their pig.

title: Coworker Suddenly Becomes Power-Mad Executive
situation: During a meeting, a coworker suddenly undergoes a personality change and starts berating Dilbert and the others as wastes of resources while boasting about his own importance. The Boss calls for an executive recruiter, who arrives and weighs whether the outburst is leadership or ordinary madness, then declares the man one of theirs while rifling through Dilbert's wallet.
punchline: The company treats a coworker's sudden arrogant, abusive outburst as a possible sign of executive talent, so the recruiter claims him for management and helps himself to everyone else's belongings.
summary: A meeting attendee abruptly turns into a bullying egomaniac, prompting management to summon a recruiter who can't tell whether he's a born leader or simply unhinged.

title: Wizard of Oz Headcount Request
situation: Wally pours coffee into the top of Dilbert's head, which is opened like the Tin Man's, joking that the Wizard can give him some ambition. Dilbert then asks if Wally fears the wicked witch's winged cat, which confuses Wally. In the last panel Alice, styled as the wicked witch with her winged cat Catbert beside her, demands headcount for her project.
punchline: The Wicked Witch's winged-monkey threat is recast as an angry manager demanding staff for her project, implying that a boss hunting for headcount is as menacing as a fairy-tale villain.
summary: In an Oz-themed office, a colleague tops up a tin-man-like coworker with coffee before the wicked witch appears wanting people for her project.

title: Project Plan Too Stupid To Read
situation: Carol brings Alice her project plan, saying Dilbert and Wally won't support it, and asks Alice to look it over. Alice reads it and reacts with violent horror, collapsing back in her chair and gurgling. Carol is left wondering why no one can just say plainly that the plan won't work.
punchline: Carol's plan is so obviously terrible that Alice is physically overcome by reading it, yet Carol still wants a polite, simple 'this won't work' instead of dramatic reactions.
summary: A colleague asks Alice to review her rejected plan and Alice is nearly incapacitated by how foolish it is.

title: Punching Ken as Non-Monetary Reward
situation: The Boss tells Alice that, because the budget is tight, her reward will be non-monetary. He offers her the chance to punch Ken from marketing as hard as she likes. Alice asks whether Ken knows, and the Boss, now at the door, says people love surprises.
punchline: Instead of a raise, the Boss offers Alice permission to assault a coworker, and he cheerfully insists the unsuspecting victim will enjoy the surprise.
summary: With no money for raises, a manager pays his employee off with a licence to slug a colleague who hasn't been warned.

title: Generic Leadership and Fake Conference Calls
situation: Dilbert explains a problem to the Boss, who admits in his thoughts that his brain has shut down for the afternoon and he has no idea what Dilbert is saying. The Boss responds with a string of generic management buzzwords, then announces a conference call as an excuse to push Dilbert out of his office. Alone, he marvels at how useful fake conference calls are.
punchline: The Boss uses empty management jargon and a fake conference call to escape a conversation he doesn't understand, then wonders how managers ever coped without such an excuse.
summary: A clueless manager fends off an employee's problem with canned buzzwords and then shoves him out the door under the pretense of a phone meeting.

title: Marketing's Data Comes From Guts
situation: Dilbert asks a marketing colleague, whose hair is shaped like two pointed horns, whether marketing has any data on customer preferences. The colleague grunts and strains, then produces a sheet of paper, implying he has just passed the 'data' from his body. Dilbert is horrified.
punchline: Marketing's customer data is literally produced by grunting and straining, implying it is made up or comes straight from their backside.
summary: Asked for real customer information, a marketer physically strains and produces a paper, leaving his coworker appalled.

title: Dogbert's Absurd Value Claims Consulting
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant called the Quantifier, is asked by the Boss how to quantify the benefits of his department. Dogbert advises making absurd claims of value and hoping nobody asks questions. When the Boss asks if that works, Dogbert admits he only hopes so and hands over his invoice.
punchline: Dogbert's advice is to bluff, and he is bluffing himself: he has no idea whether it works but still bills for the consultation.
summary: A consultant dog tells a manager to justify his department with baseless boasts, then confesses he is merely hoping it works while charging for the tip.

title: Winner's Mentality Needs Dumb Optimism
situation: Catbert, acting as the evil human resources director, tells Asok he needs a more winner-like mentality. Asok points out that a real winner wouldn't be working at this company. Catbert replies that the company actually wants employees who are both dumb and optimistic.
punchline: Asok's logic that winners wouldn't work there is confirmed by Catbert, who admits the company prefers naive, hopeful employees who don't know any better.
summary: A corporate HR cat demands a winning attitude from an employee, then reveals the company's real wish is for cheerful foolishness.

title: Saving the Planet With Bad Advice
situation: Dogbert walks with Dilbert and explains two ways to help the environment: driving an efficient car, or giving terrible career advice to someone so he loses his job and stops commuting. Dogbert then sits on a rock with Dilbert and advises him to become a real estate agent, and Dilbert naively asks 'Really?'
punchline: Dogbert is describing his plan out loud while carrying it out on Dilbert, who doesn't realize he is the idiot being set up to get fired for the sake of the planet.
summary: Dogbert cheerfully lays out an eco-friendly scheme of ruining a gullible person's career, then promptly starts applying it to Dilbert.

title: Coworkers Abandon Alice at Meeting
situation: Alice complains to Dilbert and Asok that the Boss is forcing the team to use old technology to make funding easier. They urge her to raise it at the meeting and promise to back her up. When she does, everyone, including them, denies agreeing with her, and then they switch to defending the old technology.
punchline: Her coworkers promise to support her but abandon her the moment she speaks up, a routine act of cowardly betrayal that Alice shrugs off as simply what they do.
summary: A promise of backup from colleagues evaporates the instant a complaint is voiced to management, leaving one person hanging.

title: Sadist Fails to Insult Wally
situation: Alice, in her sadist role, hurls an insult at Wally, calling him worthless and overpaid. Wally, holding his coffee mug, calmly thanks her as though it were a compliment. Frustrated that her cruelty has no effect, Alice turns the tables and asks what it's like being underpaid.
punchline: Wally is so proud of being a lazy, overpaid slacker that insults register as praise, leaving Alice's sadism powerless and her only retort an accidental admission about her own pay.
summary: A cruel coworker's attempt to wound a lazy colleague backfires when he accepts her insult as a compliment and she ends up complaining about her own pay.

title: Too Many Chair Adjustments, Disabled
situation: Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, tells the Boss that his new chair has a huge number of adjustment options. He worries that he must be using it wrong and that it may be harming him. In the last panel he stands hunched and crooked in front of the Boss and asks whether his posture looks normal.
punchline: The overly adjustable ergonomic chair has left Dilbert so contorted that he can barely stand straight, and he asks the oblivious Boss to judge whether his twisted posture is normal.
summary: A man with a hyper-adjustable new chair fears he has set it up wrongly and shows his boss the crooked posture it has left him with.

title: Electric Cubicle Walls Shock Leaner
situation: An employee walks into Dogbert's store, which sells electric cubicle walls, and says he wants to stun a coworker who keeps leaning into his cubicle without killing him. Dogbert recommends the 'Keith Richards model.' In the last panel the leaning coworker is violently electrocuted, hair on end, while the customer peeks from behind the wall and thinks he should turn it down.
punchline: The electric wall is so powerful that the coworker is left looking like Keith Richards, and the customer realises he has overdone it.
summary: A man buys an electrified cubicle wall to discourage a nosy coworker, only to find the zap is far more brutal than he intended.

title: Dogbert Picks Dumb Juror
situation: Dogbert, acting as the one questioning prospective jurors, asks a man with big eyebrows whether he is as dumb as he looks. The man answers that he cannot remember what he looks like, which proves how gullible he is. Dogbert accepts him onto the jury and adds an odd remark about being the only one who ever loved him.
punchline: Dogbert deliberately picks the dimmest juror and then plants a bit of flattery-like manipulation, implying the juror can be easily swayed to favor him.
summary: A canine interviewer seats the most simple-minded candidate on a jury and slips in a line meant to win his loyalty.

title: Wally Leaves Early, Teaches Management
situation: The Boss catches Wally leaving at four o'clock. Wally argues that genius can't be scheduled and asks to be judged by accomplishments rather than hours. When the Boss agrees and asks what Wally accomplished today, Wally claims he just taught the Boss to be a better manager.
punchline: Wally cleverly turns the Boss's own agreement to judge by accomplishments into a self-serving claim, implying that the Boss's management improvement is Wally's accomplishment and that the Boss is too incompetent to improve on his own.
summary: An employee heading home early talks his manager into judging results over hours, then cites the manager's own lesson as his big achievement of the day.

title: Determinist Blames Universe's Origin
situation: At a meeting, the Boss asks for the root cause of a failed project. Dilbert answers as a determinist, claiming the failure traces back to the origin of the universe. When the Boss asks why he is like this, Dilbert says his cubicle has destroyed his belief in free will.
punchline: Dilbert dodges accountability for the failure with philosophical determinism, and the real reason for his bleak outlook is that cubicle life has convinced him he has no free will.
summary: Asked to find the root cause of a failed project, Dilbert traces it back to the beginning of time and blames his cubicle for his fatalism.

title: Blind Squirrels and Redundant Assignments
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he gave the same assignment to every employee who resembles him. He explains this with a blind squirrel analogy, implying that many unskilled workers will eventually stumble on a solution. Dilbert then 'corrects' the insult by politely rewording it as vision-impaired squirrels.
punchline: The Boss's attempt to soften his insult by swapping 'blind' for 'vision-impaired' does nothing to remove the actual insult, that Dilbert and his lookalikes are lucky incompetents.
summary: A manager assigns identical work to a crowd of employees, compares them to sightless rodents hoping for luck, and then only polishes the wording of the slight.

title: Garbage Slides Become Company Strategy
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that his PowerPoint slides so impressed the executives that the company is overhauling its whole strategy. Dilbert honestly admits the slides were just garbage made to look good. The Boss takes this as a cue to announce that garbage is exactly what the new product line will be.
punchline: The company is staking its strategy and new product line on something Dilbert admits is worthless but well-presented, showing how style over substance drives executive decisions.
summary: A manager happily reveals that a deceptively polished presentation has convinced leadership to build the company's future on junk.

title: Dogbert's Extravagant Coach Class Plan
situation: Dogbert, as CEO, announces at a meeting that he will sacrifice by flying coach until the company is profitable again. He then lists elaborate demands, including three seats, a sherpa for his bedding, a personal air marshal and a videographer, that make his coach travel far more costly than first class.
punchline: Dogbert's 'sacrifice' of flying coach comes with so many extravagant add-ons that it undermines the cost-cutting gesture entirely.
summary: A CEO pledges to fly economy to save money, then piles on so many luxury extras that the pledge means nothing.

title: Victory Feels Like a Damp Mattress
situation: The Boss announces to his team that the company has won a huge government contract. He then explains that this means complying with all company policies plus every government procurement rule. Dilbert complains of feeling smothered, and the Boss cheerfully insists that this is what victory feels like.
punchline: Winning a government contract is really a prize of overwhelming bureaucracy, and the oblivious Boss presents the suffocating burden as the sensation of success.
summary: A triumphant announcement of a big government deal quickly turns into a pile of extra rules, and the boss insists the suffocation is the reward.

title: Don't Stir the Kettle of Crazy
situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, tells Tina she can no longer work from home because the administrative staff cannot do so and are jealous. Tina reasonably suggests he explain to the admins that her technical writing job is different from theirs. The Boss refuses, saying it is best not to stir up crazy people.
punchline: The Boss would rather take away a legitimate employee benefit than confront the unreasonable admins, preferring to punish the reasonable person to avoid dealing with the irrational ones.
summary: Rather than confront jealous coworkers, a manager strips a sensible employee of her work-from-home arrangement and justifies it with a folksy metaphor.

title: Fiddling With Boss's Life Support
situation: A doctor explains to Dilbert, Alice and Wally that the Boss survived an accident because his pointy hair cushioned the impact. He warns them not to play with the life-support machines, but Alice suggests making the Boss smarter and Wally starts poking at the equipment asking what a control does.
punchline: Despite a warning not to touch the equipment keeping the Boss alive, his coworkers immediately start tinkering with it, showing they care more about experimenting than his wellbeing.
summary: Coworkers gathered around the Boss's hospital bed ignore a doctor's plea and start experimenting with the machines keeping him alive.

title: Ombudsman Is a Soul-Buying Devil
situation: An employee asks the new ombudsman, a red devil, how he can be impartial in a dispute with management when management pays him. The devil hints that the employee could sway him by handing over something of value, implicitly his soul. Afterward, the soulless employee stands with Dilbert and Wally, and Wally remarks that he is creepy but enviably carefree.
punchline: The ombudsman is a literal devil whose price for taking your side is your soul, and the soulless employee ends up creepy but strangely carefree, so Wally envies him.
summary: A devilish workplace mediator trades his impartiality for the complainant's soul, leaving a vacant but untroubled colleague.

title: Integration Layer Boasting Coworker Condescends
situation: A bald coworker at a meeting brags about mapping applications to domains and defining interfaces, then belittles what everyone else did that week. He stands and holds his hand high above the Boss's head to show how lofty his work is in the 'integration layer'. The Boss, puzzled by the jargon, wonders what the coworker has been reading.
punchline: The coworker's pompous technical jargon is so buzzword-laden that even the Boss suspects he is just parroting something from a book or article to sound superior.
summary: A smug colleague uses lofty architecture buzzwords to put down his peers, and the Boss quietly suspects he picked it all up from a book.

title: Boss Steals Invention With Coffee Cup
situation: A scientist in a lab coat proudly explains his new mood-reading music device to the Boss, who is holding a coffee cup. The Boss throws the cup at the scientist's head, knocking him out. He then takes the device and claims it as his own invention.
punchline: The Boss resorts to violence and outright theft to take credit for someone else's invention instead of doing any real work himself.
summary: A manager knocks out an inventor with a flying mug and then proudly presents the stolen gadget as his own creation.

title: Crunching Chips Into the Speakerphone
situation: In a meeting, Dilbert tells a coworker it's a bad idea to eat a noisy bag of chips next to the speakerphone. The coworker, feeling his ego wounded, defiantly crunches away anyway. Afterward Asok asks if Dilbert really expected him to stop, and Dilbert reveals he wanted the chips to be loud.
punchline: Dilbert deliberately used reverse psychology, knowing his warning would provoke the coworker into crunching louder, because he dislikes the person on the speakerphone.
summary: A gentle warning about snack noise turns out to be a calculated trick to torment a disliked caller.

title: Wally's Fake Data Philosophy
situation: In a meeting, the Boss asks Asok for reliability statistics on the previous model. Asok says the data doesn't exist, so the Boss sends him to Wally, who teaches him to simply type random numbers into a spreadsheet. Wally justifies his laziness with a faux-philosophical claim about enlightenment.
punchline: Wally dresses up his laziness and data fabrication as profound wisdom, arguing that enlightened beings never exert effort, as proven by the absence of jogging Buddha statues.
summary: A young engineer is taught by his laziest coworker to fabricate missing data with made-up numbers, justified by a pseudo-spiritual rationalization.

title: Alice Disposes of Boss Through Portal
situation: Asok proudly explains that his portal to a parallel universe succeeded because Alice killed their boss, which made everyone more productive. Alice shoves him aside because the police are investigating and she needs to retrieve something from the other universe. She then pushes the boss's head through the portal and tells a horrified Asok that another universe just became more productive.
punchline: Alice gets rid of the incriminating evidence by shoving it into another universe, and treats it as a favor since the boss's absence boosts productivity there too.
summary: A scientist's portal to another universe becomes a handy way for a murderous coworker to dump the evidence, with a grim silver lining for the universe next door.

title: Dogbert Teaches Toxic Workplace Behavior
situation: Dogbert stands on a stool teaching a roomful of employees how to be toxic, advising them to stir up fights and complain about personal problems. He assigns homework to practice at work the next day. In the final panel, a coworker eagerly applies the lesson at a meeting by telling Alice that Dilbert thinks her plan is lame, while Dilbert looks alarmed and Alice glares angrily.
punchline: The employees immediately turn Dogbert's toxicity lesson into practice, sabotaging a colleague and stirring up conflict, proving that workplace toxicity is easy to learn and spread.
summary: A canine trainer coaches office workers to become poisonous colleagues, and one of them instantly starts a feud at the next meeting.

title: Checking Email During Conversation Standoff
situation: Alice tells Dilbert that his conversation is boring her and pulls out her phone to check email while he talks. Dilbert responds by pulling out his own phone and glaring at her, while Alice suspects he is now emailing her. The exchange turns into a tense, petty standoff.
punchline: Alice rudely admits she is bored and checks her email mid-conversation, but she is instantly offended when Dilbert does the same thing back, showing her double standard.
summary: A woman openly ignores a coworker for her phone, then bristles when he retaliates by doing exactly the same thing.

title: Replace You With Moss
situation: At a meeting, a bald executive boasts that the company needs a succession plan because he is so awesome and charismatic. Alice replies that he never invented anything and could be replaced by a bag of moss. He falls silent, and Alice points out that this proves moss could do his job.
punchline: The executive's sudden silence proves that a bag of moss could fill his role, since it too would just sit there quietly.
summary: A self-important executive demands a succession plan, and a colleague shuts him up by suggesting a bag of moss could replace him.

title: Piranha Flu Sneeze Gone Wrong
situation: A woman in a pink sweater tells a male coworker holding a coffee mug that she has a wicked case of piranha flu. She sneezes, and a swarm of angry piranhas flies out and strips the coworker down to a skeleton. She then remarks that she should probably tell people it is just bad allergies.
punchline: Her sneeze literally releases flesh-eating piranhas that kill her coworker, and she casually worries about how to explain it away as ordinary allergies.
