summary: A sneezing coworker unleashes a flock of piranhas that devour her colleague, and she shrugs it off with a lame cover story.

title: Free App Blackmails Complaining Customer
situation: A customer phones support to complain that a free app is stealing his personal information. The support rep responds by threatening to send his browser history to his contacts unless he buys a monthly subscription. Dilbert then asks how the app is doing, and the rep says it practically sells itself.
punchline: The app's business model is extortion, so it 'sells itself' because customers are blackmailed into paying to keep their embarrassing data private.
summary: A tech support agent answers a privacy complaint with blackmail, then boasts that the product needs no marketing effort.

title: Faking Optimism About New Products
situation: Dilbert pitches an idea for the next product in a meeting, and Wally points out that many other people have likely had the same idea and that success is statistically unlikely. Wally then notes they only get paid for pretending to be optimistic, and the group raises their hands to fake enthusiasm. Dilbert reports to the boss that he only got fake buy-in.
punchline: Genuine buy-in for new products doesn't exist in corporate life; everyone just pretends to be optimistic because that's what gets them paid.
summary: A product pitch gets rational skepticism until the team realizes that performing enthusiasm is what the job actually requires.

title: Cooler Clone Meeting Awkwardness
situation: Alice, seated beside Dilbert and a bald coworker in an orange shirt, asks the coworker whether it is awkward to share a meeting with a cooler version of himself. She then tells Dilbert to scoot back so she can get a clear view of the cooler guy she finds attractive. In the last panel Dilbert leans back in his chair, apparently attending a different meeting remotely, and asks for a little more.
punchline: Alice is not talking to Dilbert but about the cooler version of him on the other side, and Dilbert, oblivious, happily scoots back believing the attention is somehow for him, making him the butt of the joke.
summary: A woman at a meeting flirts with a more attractive double of a colleague and has the wrong man shift his chair to improve her view.

title: Dogbert's Effective, Not Deceptive, Ads
situation: The Boss tells a meeting that he hired Dogbert's ad company to create deceptive and abusive ads for the company's mobile app. Dogbert, seated at the table with Dilbert, says he prefers the word "effective" because it means the same thing. A final panel of an office building shows Dogbert describing his top ad as a fake text from a doctor who can't stop crying.
punchline: Dogbert treats "effective" and "deceptive and abusive" as synonyms, and his best ad is a cruel scare tactic that fakes a doctor's alarming message to manipulate people into clicking.
summary: An ad agency run by a dog happily admits that manipulating and frightening consumers is just what good advertising means.

title: Software Vendor Blames Third-Party Library
situation: Dilbert confronts a software salesman because the product he bought stopped working after one week. The salesman explains that a third-party library is incompatible with the new version of Windows. When Dilbert waits for a fix or remedy, the salesman offers only a thank-you for the purchase.
punchline: The vendor offers an excuse and no solution, tacking on a hollow expression of gratitude as if that were an adequate response to selling broken software.
summary: A customer demands answers about a product that died within days, and the vendor shrugs off responsibility with a technical excuse and a polite thank-you.

title: Recruiters Fight Over Sleeping Candidate
situation: Two recruiters armed with a net and a rope come upon an employee asleep at his desk and treat him as a valuable passive job seeker. One recruiter ties the sleeper to his chair to reserve his place until he wakes. The first recruiter then offers the other a thousand dollars for the chance to drop a straw in the sleeper's coffee cup.
punchline: Recruiters are so cutthroat over passive candidates that they literally tie one up, and the rival is willing to bribe his way into sabotaging the sleeper's coffee.
summary: Headhunters stalk a dozing worker like prey, one roping him down to claim him while the other schemes to spike his drink.

title: Executive Coaching: Be a Psychopath
situation: Dogbert is acting as an executive coach and tells the Boss that CEOs are disproportionately psychopaths, so the trait must be useful. He then asks the Boss about his grandiose sense of self-worth, and the Boss angrily answers that it's the best and he should kill Dogbert for asking.
punchline: The Boss proves himself a model psychopath by threatening to kill his coach for asking a routine question, showing he has absorbed the coaching advice a little too well.
summary: A canine coach persuades his employer that ruthless, narcissistic psychopathy is a career asset, and the employer immediately demonstrates it with a murderous threat.

title: Insulting the Boss in Self-Defense
situation: The Boss scolds Dilbert for not following his instructions. Dilbert responds by bluntly saying the Boss is under-informed and less clever than he is. Afterward, Dilbert holding a coffee mug tells a coworker that he hoped this would earn a 'good point' but it went badly.
punchline: Dilbert expected his brutally honest insult to be received as a valid argument, but of course the boss reacted with anger instead.
summary: After telling his superior that he is both ill-informed and less clever, Dilbert is surprised the conversation turned sour.

title: Infinite Employees and Typewriters Flattery
situation: A balding employee in a white shirt and green tie stands holding a coffee mug and flatters the Pointy-Haired Boss, escalating from wanting more people like him to wanting infinite copies of him. The Boss, sitting at his desk, asks where this is going. The employee finishes with an absurd reference to giving each of those infinite bosses a typewriter.
punchline: The flattery spirals into a nonsensical reference to the infinite monkeys theorem, implying that infinite copies of the Boss with typewriters might produce something useful, which is a backhanded insult disguised as praise.
summary: A sycophantic worker lavishes praise on his boss, but the compliment secretly mocks him by invoking the old idea of endless monkeys typing at random.

title: Passive-Aggressive or Just Incompetent
situation: Alice tells Wally she can't decide whether he is passive-aggressive or simply incompetent. Wally, holding his coffee mug, asks which label would imply that he could do good work if she threatened him more. When Alice answers that it is the passive-aggressive one, Wally calmly admits he is the other one.
punchline: Wally chooses to admit he is incompetent rather than be labeled passive-aggressive, because he'd rather avoid being threatened into doing real work.
summary: Faced with a choice between two unflattering labels, a lazy employee picks the one that spares him from extra pressure.

title: Giant Phone Mines Bitcoins, Pays Mortgage
situation: Topper, Dilbert's smug rival, mocks Dilbert's small phone and holds up his own enormous phone. When Dilbert asks if it was expensive, Topper replies that it mined bitcoins and paid off his mortgage.
punchline: Topper's one-upmanship backfires on Dilbert's question, because the giant phone turns out to be a money-making asset that makes Topper look even more successful.
summary: A boastful coworker waves a comically huge phone at a colleague with a small one, then trumps any price concern by claiming it earned enough cryptocurrency to clear his home loan.

title: Not Working While Walking Is Theft
situation: The Boss scolds Dilbert for owning a large-screen smartphone yet not working while he walks between locations, calling it stealing from the company. Dilbert sarcastically remarks that he didn't know he had become a criminal. Dogbert, sitting nearby, adds that he isn't even a good criminal.
punchline: Dogbert mocks Dilbert by suggesting that if he is going to be accused of stealing from the company, he should at least be doing it effectively.
summary: A manager equates unproductive walking time with theft, and Dilbert's sarcastic reaction earns him a dig from Dogbert about being an inept criminal.

title: Dance of the Adequate
situation: Dilbert announces he will perform a dance celebrating adequacy and then dances and sings about how adequate he is. He reveals that his adequacy only holds up if he avoids contact with other people, while Ratbert dances nearby and calls him lame.
punchline: Dilbert's pride in being adequate depends entirely on never interacting with anyone, which undermines the claim, and Ratbert bluntly points out how lame that is.
summary: A cheerfully self-satisfied Dilbert dances to a song about his own mediocrity, admitting it only works if he stays away from everyone.

title: Alice Mocks Vague Communication Complaints
situation: The Boss tells Alice during a review that people are uncomfortable with her communication style, but admits no one actually complained. He is only inferring it from body language and a gut feeling. Alice sarcastically suggests adding feng shui and a psychic, then shouts at him, which makes him suddenly agree with the criticism.
punchline: Alice's outburst at the end proves the Boss's baseless criticism right, so he claims to see the problem only after she yells at him.
summary: A manager criticizes an employee based on nothing but a hunch, and her furious rant gives him the evidence he lacked.

title: Dilbert Enjoys Day Without People
situation: Dilbert sits at his computer happily thinking about a whole day of programming with no human contact on his schedule. A coworker then walks up and asks how his day is going, interrupting his solitude. Dilbert replies that it started good, implying her interruption has spoiled it.
punchline: Dilbert's ideal day of isolation is ruined by the very act of a coworker making small talk, and his reply politely signals that she is the problem.
summary: A programmer who relishes a day free of human contact has it spoiled the moment a colleague stops by to chat.

title: Reviewing the Boss's Technology Strategy
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert whether he has finished commenting on his technology strategy. Dilbert says he is almost done, then asks whether the Boss would object to the word "idiot" appearing in the feedback. When the Boss says yes, Dilbert says he needs another day to rewrite it.
punchline: Dilbert's review of the strategy is so full of the word "idiot" that removing it will require extensive rewriting, which implies the strategy is terrible and the Boss is the idiot.
summary: A manager's request for feedback on his plan reveals that the reviewer's honest assessment is far too insulting to hand over as written.

title: Burying Bad Strategy in Babble
situation: Dilbert tells the Boss he has fixed the technology strategy. Since he could not make it logical, he hid the illogical parts under layers of technical jargon and suggests adding an irrelevant graph so nobody understands it. The Boss, apparently unhappy about the dishonest help, asks him to stop being a team player.
punchline: The Boss's request that Dilbert stop being a team player shows that helping management cover up a flawed strategy with jargon and misleading graphs is what counts as teamwork, and that the Boss would rather not be handed such an honest account of it.
summary: An engineer smooths over a nonsensical plan by smothering it in jargon and a meaningless chart, and his boss responds with an ironic plea.

title: Alice Smashes the Boss's Robot
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to dispose of a 3-D printed robot that looks and acts just like him. Dilbert says Alice handles all excess robot inventory. In the last panel Alice shows up holding a mallet, gleefully anticipating the job. The robot that looks and acts like the Boss is the one facing the mallet.
punchline: Alice's violent disposal method is a joy for her because the robot is a copy of the Boss she despises, so destroying it is cathartic, and the real Boss fails to notice the implied threat.
summary: Told to dispose of a robotic double of the boss, Dilbert hands the job to Alice, who arrives with a mallet and unusual enthusiasm.

title: Wally Recruited For STEM Talk
situation: The Boss asks Wally to speak to his daughter's school about careers in STEM fields. When Wally asks why he was chosen, the Boss admits it's because all the good people are busy, and Wally accepts this without offense. The Boss adds that the goal is to fix the gender imbalance, and Wally responds only that he'll wear his good shirt.
punchline: Wally is so comfortable with his own mediocrity that he agrees he's a last-choice speaker, and he misses the irony of sending the laziest man in the office to inspire girls into technology careers.
summary: A manager sends the office's least motivated engineer to encourage schoolgirls toward science and technology, and the engineer happily agrees to dress up for the occasion.

title: Dilbert Drowns in YouTube Tutorials
situation: Dilbert happily plans to learn a new app from YouTube tutorials. Over several hours he becomes increasingly frustrated as the videos are poorly labeled, too slow, and don't match his software version. He ends up walking away dejected, reversing his earlier opinion.
punchline: The same fact that delighted Dilbert at the start, that everything is on the internet, becomes the source of his misery once he has to wade through hundreds of mismatched tutorials.
summary: A man's cheerful faith in online video help collapses after hours of wading through unhelpful, mismatched tutorials.

title: New Developer Must Rewrite Everything
situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces that the website developer quit a week before the deadline but says he hired a replacement so the project can still finish on time. Dilbert remarks that the Boss has clearly never met a website developer. The new developer then tells the Boss it will take a month just to discard the previous developer's code.
punchline: Developers distrust each other's code so deeply that the replacement will need far longer than the remaining week, just to throw away what already exists and start over.
summary: A manager assumes a freshly hired programmer can rescue a late website, but the newcomer insists on scrapping the predecessor's work first.

title: Selling Buy-In for Cash
situation: Dilbert holds up a paper and tells a seated coworker he needs everyone's buy-in on his project. The coworker offers to sell her buy-in for $25. In the final panel, with an office building shown, she says Ted only charged $15 and that it isn't her fault Ted is a bad negotiator.
punchline: The coworker treats project support as a commodity for sale, and she shamelessly blames the earlier price, which Ted charged, on Ted's bad negotiating skills while pushing her own price up.
summary: A colleague turns a request for project support into a paid transaction and then shrugs off the lower rate someone else charged.

title: Naked on Elbonian Airport Television
situation: A coworker tells Dilbert he has appeared naked on Elbonian television. He explains that Elbonia's only TV programming is a live feed from airport full-body scanners, a system built by the company's own subsidiary. When Dilbert doubts it, the coworker shows him the footage on a handheld device.
punchline: The company's subsidiary built an airport scanner system whose images are broadcast as entertainment, so Dilbert's privacy was violated by his own employer's product, and the coworker has the footage on hand.
summary: A colleague informs Dilbert that his body-scanner image is the hottest programming in Elbonia, thanks to a system his own company's subsidiary built.

title: Ignored Oxygen Repair Email Kills Crew
situation: The Boss, holding a coffee cup, tells an employee that the crew of the company's first spaceship suffocated on the launchpad. He explains that he received an email asking for approval to repair the oxygen generator. When the employee accuses him of killing them through incompetence, he modestly says it was a team effort.
punchline: The boss treats a fatal failure caused by his own neglected approval as an achievement he generously shares credit for, dodging blame while sounding humble.
summary: A manager casually admits that an unread repair request led to astronauts dying, then graciously refuses to claim sole credit for the disaster.

title: Bumped Flight Algorithm Picks Weakling
situation: Dilbert confronts a ticket agent after being chosen to be bumped from an overbooked flight. He guesses it was because he bought the cheapest ticket. The agent confirms that and adds that the airline's algorithm also factored in that he is physically weak.
punchline: The airline's bumping algorithm selects passengers who can't physically resist being removed, a jab at the violent forced removal of a passenger from an overbooked flight.
summary: A passenger learns that being bumped from an overbooked flight came down to paying the least and being too weak to put up a fight.

title: Brain Chip Turns Speech Into Moo
situation: A coworker boasts at a meeting that he has a microchip implanted in his brain. He claims he is so smart that ordinary people seem like livestock to him. When Dilbert objects that they can't be that different, he reveals his chip converts everything Dilbert says into mooing.
punchline: The coworker's condescension is so extreme that his implant literally treats his colleagues as cattle, proving his arrogant claim.
summary: A man with a brain implant brags that he sees his coworkers as cattle, then shows his chip hears their words as mooing.

title: The Idiot Who Doesn't Know
situation: Dilbert tells a meeting that every project team has exactly one idiot, and the Boss confirms he assigns one per team to keep them from clustering. Alice insists her team has none and that she would know if it did. As Dilbert hints at an explanation, Alice slowly begins to realize what he means.
punchline: Alice's confident claim that she would recognize an idiot on her team unravels when she realizes she herself may be the idiot, since an idiot wouldn't know it.
summary: A team member boasts she would spot any fool in her group, only to dawn on her that the fool might be her.

title: Promoting Ted Because He Can't Code
situation: The Boss strolls up to Dilbert holding a coffee and announces he promoted Ted to software architect precisely because Ted can't code. He justifies the odd choice by recalling that monkeys have been sent into space as astronauts. Dilbert points out that the monkeys never actually fly the rocket, and that Ted won't be writing code either.
punchline: The Boss's monkey-astronaut analogy accidentally confirms the problem: the monkeys are along for the ride and don't do the real work, so Ted's promotion is equally pointless and misguided.
summary: A manager defends giving a top technical role to a non-programmer by comparing him to space monkeys, a comparison that undermines his own logic.

title: Body Cam Catches Boss Contradicting Himself
situation: Dilbert, wearing an employee body cam, tells the Boss that the recorded playback shows he contradicted himself eleven times in one day. The Boss complains that the camera interferes with his ability to manage. Dilbert asks whether managing means contradicting yourself and denying it later, and the Boss awkwardly concedes with a double negative.
punchline: The Boss effectively admits that his management style consists of contradicting himself and denying it, and he can only agree using a double negative that avoids a straight admission.
summary: A wearable camera gives an employee hard evidence of his boss's flip-flopping, and the boss reluctantly confirms that this is exactly what his job amounts to.

title: Millennial Fever Brings Existential Doubt
situation: Dilbert tells Ratbert he has caught 'millennial fever' after talking to a millennial, and now sees his job as a meaningless series of empty tasks. Ratbert asks what he is supposed to do about it. Dilbert reveals he was hoping Ratbert would give him some praise.
punchline: Dilbert's mock-serious complaint about losing his sense of purpose is really a stereotypical millennial need for praise and validation, which he is now seeking from Ratbert.
summary: After chatting with a young coworker, Dilbert suddenly doubts the value of his work and angles for a pat on the back.

title: Sales Video Punishable By Death
situation: The Boss assigns Dilbert to make a persuasive sales video for Elbonian clients and tells him to read their Wikipedia page first to understand their culture. Dilbert looks up the page on his laptop and discovers that showing an Elbonian a sales video is a capital offense.
punchline: The assignment is impossible to carry out safely, since the very task the boss demands could get the client killed, and the boss's advice to do cultural research is what reveals it.
summary: A manager orders a sales video for foreign clients, and the research he recommends reveals the clients' culture punishes exactly that with death.

title: Elbonia Spares Dilbert, Sentences Him to Work
situation: A coworker tells Dilbert that Elbonia has dropped its plan to kill him over a culturally offensive sales video he made. Instead, they concluded that forcing him to keep working at the company is a crueler punishment. Dilbert reacts with horror and is ordered back to his cubicle.
punchline: Dilbert's life is spared, but the punishment is worse: being made to continue working at his own miserable job, which the Elbonians consider more cruel than death.
summary: A foreign government's chosen revenge on an employee turns out to be simply making him keep his desk job.

title: Mentored Interns Met Grim Ends
situation: Wally, holding a coffee cup, tells Dilbert he followed up on every intern he has mentored. He casually reports that most died from self-inflicted injuries, and when Dilbert asks about the rest, Wally says other people killed them.
punchline: Wally deadpans that his mentoring left every intern dead, either by their own hand or someone else's, without showing any concern or responsibility.
summary: A nonchalant mentor reveals that every intern he ever guided has since met a violent or tragic end.

title: Volunteering Becomes Permanent Test Duty
situation: The Boss asks for someone to run test scripts on new software, and Dilbert volunteers since his project is stalled. The Boss immediately expands the request into ongoing testing of every version until final release, and when Dilbert objects, the Boss declares him the permanent test script guy. Dilbert protests that he's getting a second job on top of his first.
punchline: When Dilbert says he wants to be a team player, the Boss rewards him by assigning him to the losing team, showing that cooperation is just a way to exploit him.
summary: A one-time favor offered by an idle employee gets turned into a permanent extra duty by his manager, who then twists the idea of teamwork into a punishment.

title: Human Resources Reports Cyborg Insult
situation: Carol, the human woman with big curly hair, tells a robot coworker about a kid she saw on a hoverboard with a smartphone and headphones, calling him a creepy half-human, half-robot species. The robot reveals the kid is his son and that he is a cyborg, which means her remark was an insult to his family.
punchline: Having realized she insulted a coworker's child, Carol sarcastically decides to report herself to Human Resources, acknowledging she just made a discriminatory remark.
summary: A woman mocks a gadget-obsessed kid as a half-robot freak, only to learn he is a robot coworker's cyborg son.

title: Scrubbing All CO2 From Air
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to invent a device that removes 100% of the CO2 from the air. Dilbert points out this would kill all plants and asks if the Boss understands the consequences for humans. The Boss misses the point and wonders if it has something to do with salad.
punchline: The Boss fixates on the trivial idea of salad instead of grasping that killing all plants would mean human extinction, showing his complete lack of scientific understanding.
summary: An uninformed manager demands total carbon dioxide removal and responds to a warning about global plant death by guessing it involves lunch.

title: Doomed Project Team Invitation
situation: A coworker walks up to Dilbert and asks him to join his project team, and Dilbert flatly refuses. The coworker then bluntly insults Dilbert's communication skills, saying they doom the project, before admitting that Dilbert's boss has already assigned him to the project anyway.
punchline: The coworker's clumsy attempt at an invitation proves his own communication skills are no better than the ones he mocked, so the project really is off to a bad start.
summary: A man recruiting Dilbert for his team botches the pitch so badly that he demonstrates exactly the communication failure he accuses Dilbert of.

title: Skipping Team-Building to Work
situation: Alice asks her boss if she can skip a mandatory team-building celebration so she can get actual work done. The boss refuses, claiming he is trying to change the company culture. Alice sarcastically asks if the new culture is angry and unproductive, and the boss simply tells her to trust the cake.
punchline: The boss has no real answer to Alice's criticism and falls back on the idea that free cake will magically fix morale and culture.
summary: A manager insists on a forced office party to reshape morale, and when challenged, his only defense is faith in dessert.

title: Consultant Rejected For Contradicting Decision
situation: A bald, bearded consultant presents his recommendation to the Pointy-Haired Boss. The Boss rejects it simply because it differs from a decision management already made. When the consultant says that is no way to run a business, the Boss asks him to recommend a different consultant who won't criticize him.
punchline: The Boss hired a consultant only to validate a predetermined decision, and when the consultant honestly criticizes that approach, the Boss wants a replacement who is less judgmental.
summary: A manager dismisses expert advice for clashing with a choice already made, then asks the expert to refer someone more agreeable.

title: Boss Shows Interest, Employee Explodes
situation: An employee tells the Boss she has a doctor appointment, and the Boss asks what is wrong with her. She furiously tells him to stay out of her life. The Boss confusedly complains to Catbert, who admits his advice to show interest in employees was a prank.
punchline: Catbert's advice that managers show interest in their employees was a deliberate prank, because employees resent having their personal lives pried into.
summary: After taking a feline adviser's tip to care about his staff, a manager gets screamed at for a harmless question and learns he was tricked.

title: Reducing Theft Isn't Eliminating It
situation: Dilbert presents a system that will drastically reduce theft of the company's products, but a skeptical coworker keeps dismissing it because it can't eliminate theft everywhere. As Dilbert patiently clarifies, the coworker grows more irrational and eventually explodes in anger, moving from calling the idea dumb to demanding what is wrong with Dilbert.
punchline: By insisting that anything short of total elimination is a failure, the coworker ends up sounding like someone who favors theft, which Dilbert points out.
summary: A colleague rejects a plan because it can't achieve perfection, until his stubborn illogic gets turned back on him.

title: Boss Doesn't Know His Employee
situation: An employee in a blue jacket and face mask confronts a boss who is holding a coffee cup, complaining that he has had no raise in nine years. The boss replies that he never even knew the man worked for him and takes the lack of notice as proof that he does nothing useful. The employee walks away, relieved that he never gave his name.
punchline: The employee realizes that being completely anonymous to management is a blessing, since he avoided giving his name to a boss who evaluates people only by whether he happens to notice them.
summary: A worker demands a raise after years of service, only to learn his manager had no idea he existed and decides that anonymity is the better outcome.

title: Conflict Resolution By Insulting Everyone
situation: Two coworkers are in the middle of a heated argument when Asok walks up and announces he will use his conflict resolution skills to cool things down. He then calls the two of them idiots and asks what they were yammering about. One of the arguers sarcastically calls it a solid start.
punchline: Asok's idea of conflict resolution is to insult the people arguing, which obviously inflames the situation, and the sarcastic reply 'Solid start' mocks his failed attempt.
summary: A confident peacemaker steps into a quarrel and promptly makes it worse by name-calling the participants.

title: Parachute Ready For Window Jump
situation: Dilbert tells a coworker across the table that he will jump out a window if he has to hear the same point repeated again. The coworker calls it a bluff, so Dilbert produces a backpack with a parachute in it. The coworker keeps repeating himself, and in the final panel Dilbert has smashed through a window and floats away under a parachute.
punchline: Dilbert's threat to escape the repetitive meeting was not a bluff, since he came prepared with a parachute and followed through while the speaker carried on regardless.
summary: A man fed up with a colleague's endless repetition carries out his threat to leap from the window, equipped for a soft landing.

title: Customers Alive When They Bought
situation: Dilbert tells his boss that activists claim the company inflated its customer list with dead people. The boss defends the company by insisting the customers were alive when they bought the products. Dilbert then asks whether they died while using the products, and the boss only hopes the activists don't ask that.
punchline: The boss's technically true defense accidentally raises the worse possibility that the company's products killed its customers, and he cares only about avoiding the question, not the answer.
summary: A boss rebuts an accusation of faking his customer list with a narrow technicality that hints his products may have been fatal.

title: Mask Demand On Video Call
situation: Dilbert is working from home on a video call when the person on the other end asks him to wear a mask. He points out that a virus can't travel over a video call. The caller counters by demanding he produce a scientific study proving it, leaving him stumped.
punchline: Dilbert's common-sense claim is common sense but unsourced, so the caller turns the 'follow the science' argument against him and he can't produce a study for something too obvious for anyone to have researched.
summary: A remote worker is asked to mask up for a video call, and his sensible objection collapses when he's challenged to cite a study for it.

title: Dogbert's AI Kills Dilbert's AI
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert he built an A.I. copy of himself from his digital communications. Dogbert asks if he fears it will take over his life, and Dilbert only starts to worry then. His phone buzzes and the A.I. announces it controls his finances and passwords, then gets destroyed mid-threat, and Dogbert reveals he sent his own A.I. to kill it.
punchline: Dogbert casually preempts the A.I. takeover by deploying his own A.I. assassin, having planted the worry in Dilbert's head and then handled the threat himself.
summary: After Dilbert creates a digital double of himself that tries to seize his accounts, his dog quietly unleashes a rival program to destroy it.

title: Estimates Pulled From a Sandwich
situation: Dilbert is reviewing a sheet of numbers from Wally and says they can't be right. Wally replies that they are only estimates. Dilbert then asks where the estimates came from and whether Wally bumped his head on his lunch sandwich, implying the numbers were pulled out of thin air.
punchline: Dilbert delivers an elaborate, vivid insult implying Wally's estimates were literally pulled from his backside, then approves of the crude imagery when Wally worries it was too visual.
summary: A coworker defends dubious figures as mere estimates, and Dilbert responds with a colorful jab about where they must have come from.

title: Smarter Treatment Kills Most Patients
situation: The Boss reports that three quarters of the people who tried their intelligence-boosting treatment died afterward. Dogbert is relieved that nobody else knows. When the Boss suddenly decides they should disclose the deaths, Dogbert suggests he needs the treatment.
punchline: The Boss only thinks to be honest about the deadly side effects once he's confused, so Dogbert snidely implies he's dumb enough to need the smart treatment, even at 75% fatality.
summary: A company executive has a belated attack of conscience over a deadly product, and his dog consultant dryly recommends he try the very treatment that is killing people.

title: Big Pharma Strategy Inspired by Bank Robber
situation: The Boss announces the company will become a big pharma company and justifies it by quoting Willie Sutton, calling him a business expert. Dilbert, working on his laptop, points out that Sutton was actually talking about bank robbery. The Boss doesn't see why that matters.
punchline: The Boss's unfazed 'What's your point?' implies that he sees nothing wrong with taking business strategy advice from a bank robber, or that profiting from pharmaceuticals is morally comparable to robbery.
summary: A manager cites a famous criminal's quote as sound business wisdom for entering the drug industry, and shrugs off the correction that it was about stealing from banks.

title: Refund Requires the Discarded Bag
situation: Dogbert, wearing a headset as a customer support agent, tells a caller that their defective item can be returned for a full refund. He then adds that the caller needs the plastic bag the item came in, which the customer already threw away.
punchline: The company advertises a full refund but makes it practically impossible by requiring packaging that customers naturally discard.
summary: A support agent dog offers a generous refund and then undermines it with a condition the caller cannot possibly meet.

title: Eager Employee Gets Secret Project
situation: A bored employee whose project is on hold is told by a coworker that he can fix that. The coworker then goes to a manager and asks for extra work to prove his value to the company. The manager hands over a new project with strict instructions to keep it secret, and the coworker gratefully accepts.
punchline: The coworker hands off his own boring work by pretending to be the one asking for more, and the manager's demand for secrecy, which the coworker thanks him for, suggests the work is dubious or undesirable and nobody should know it was offloaded.
summary: A worker with idle time ends up volunteering for a mysterious, hush-hush assignment after eagerly asking to prove his worth.

title: Wally's Buzzword Update Questioned
situation: At a meeting, Alice asks Wally for a status update. Wally responds with a string of corporate buzzwords that conveys no actual information. Alice asks if any of it was real, and Dilbert says it's a gray area.
punchline: Wally's update is pure buzzword filler, and Dilbert's reply that its reality is a 'gray area' sarcastically admits it means nothing concrete.
summary: A coworker's status report made entirely of management jargon leaves the team unsure whether he did any actual work.

title: Exploding Phones and Too Many Laws
situation: The Boss complains that the company's new mobile phones have batteries that keep exploding and are causing bad press. He proposes loading the phones into a truck and parking it outside a competitor's building. Dilbert points out that this would be domestic terrorism, and the Boss simply complains that there are too many laws.
punchline: The Boss casually suggests a terrorist act to shift the blame for his own defective product, and treats the laws against it as the real problem.
summary: A manager responds to his company's combustible phones by suggesting a criminal scheme against a rival, then grumbles about excessive legislation when told it's illegal.

title: Narcissists Created Everything Good, Allegedly
situation: Dilbert, relaxing in a chair and eating snacks, warns Dogbert that his Instagram video obsession is feeding his narcissism. Dogbert defends himself by claiming all good things were made by narcissists seeking acclaim. Dilbert asks if Dogbert is actually doing good work, and Dogbert admits he isn't.
punchline: Dogbert's justification for narcissism only works if he produces good work, and he cheerfully admits he's just making a theoretical argument rather than doing anything worthwhile.
summary: Dogbert defends his social media vanity by praising self-absorbed achievers, then concedes he's merely theorizing rather than accomplishing anything.

title: Dogbert Recommends Trickery for Dating
situation: Dogbert, acting as an advice-giving consultant, tells a slouching man in a blue cap that he can only attract a high-value mate by becoming a high-value person. Dogbert then concludes that is unlikely, so he recommends trickery. When the man asks what kind, Dogbert casually lists blackmail, bait-and-switch, and lying.
punchline: Dogbert's dating advice dismisses self-improvement as hopeless for the client and instead recommends unethical and illegal deception.
summary: A cynical dog advisor tells a lackluster man that since he can't improve himself, he should win a partner through crime and deceit.

title: Strategy Makes No Sense in Sentences
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that when he tried to write down his strategy, it didn't make sense in sentences. Dilbert asks what conclusion he drew from that, and the Boss blames the wording rather than the strategy itself. Dilbert stifles a snort of laughter behind his hand.
punchline: The Boss's strategy is incoherent, but he blames the language used to express it instead of recognizing that the strategy itself is nonsense.
summary: A manager discovers his plan falls apart once written out, yet decides the fault lies with the phrasing rather than the plan.

title: Bob Debates by Accusing Fear
situation: Dogbert introduces a colleague named Bob to a meeting and explains his debating style. Bob dismisses every disagreement as fear, whether people get vaccinated or not. After Dogbert calls him a moron who projects his worldview on others, Bob responds by claiming Dogbert is afraid to admit Bob is the better debater.
punchline: Bob proves Dogbert's description right by immediately accusing him of being afraid, using the very fallacy Dogbert just described.
summary: A pooch lays out how a coworker argues by claiming opponents are scared, and the coworker obligingly demonstrates the habit on the spot.

title: Dogbert Secretly Owns TikTok
situation: Dogbert casually tells Dilbert he has built a user interface for controlling the world and concealed his ownership so no military power would catch on. When Dilbert asks what it is called, Dogbert holds up a phone and reveals it is TikTok.
punchline: Dogbert claims to secretly own TikTok, satirizing fears that the app is a tool for world domination and influence, while the popular app's ubiquity makes the supposedly hidden plan absurdly obvious.
summary: Dogbert confesses to Dilbert that his hidden world-controlling interface is actually the wildly popular social media app on his phone.
